title: Fundevogel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 51. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, thät und ward).
about: KHM 51, a short flight-and-transformation tale. A forester carries home a child a bird of prey had set in a treetop, and raises it beside his own Lenchen; when the old cook plans to boil the foundling, the two children run and change shape three times to escape her. Everything turns on a vow the children exchange, all but unchanged, each time danger comes near; the 1857 spelling brings gieng, fieng, daß and thäte, and the dialect nein for hinein.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Förster, der gieng in den Wald auf die Jagd, und wie er in den Wald kam, hörte er schreien, als obs ein kleines Kind wäre.
sentences.l: There was once a forester; he went into the forest to the hunt, and when he came into the forest, he heard crying, as if it were a little child.
sentences.i: There was once a forester who went out into the forest to hunt; and as he came into the forest he heard a crying, as though it were a little child.
sentences.n: “auf die Jagd gehen” = to go hunting. obs = ob es; “als ob” takes the subjunctive (wäre), “as if it were”.

sentences.t: Er gieng dem Schreien nach und kam endlich zu einem hohen Baum, und oben darauf saß ein kleines Kind.
sentences.l: He went after the crying and came at last to a tall tree, and up on top of it sat a little child.
sentences.i: He followed the crying and came at last to a tall tree, and up at the top of it sat a little child.
sentences.n: “nachgehen” takes a dative: “dem Schreien… nach”, he went after the crying.

sentences.t: Es war aber die Mutter mit dem Kinde unter dem Baum eingeschlafen, und ein Raubvogel hatte das Kind in ihrem Schooße gesehen: da war er hinzu geflogen, hatte es mit seinem Schnabel weggenommen und auf den hohen Baum gesetzt.
sentences.l: But the mother had fallen asleep with the child under the tree, and a bird of prey had seen the child in her lap: then it had flown over to them, had taken it away with its beak and set it on the tall tree.
sentences.i: The mother, though, had fallen asleep with the child under the tree, and a bird of prey had seen the child in her lap; so it had flown up, carried it off in its beak, and set it in the tall tree.
sentences.n: Schooße = modern Schoße, from Schoß, lap. Raubvogel is a “robber-bird”, a bird of prey. The mother is never mentioned again.

sentences.t: Der Förster stieg hinauf, holte das Kind herunter und dachte „du willst das Kind mit nach Haus nehmen und mit deinem Lenchen zusammen aufziehn.“
sentences.l: The forester climbed up, fetched the child down and thought “you will take the child home with you and bring it up together with your Lenchen.”
sentences.i: The forester climbed up, fetched the child down, and thought: “You shall take the child home with you and raise it together with your Lenchen.”
sentences.n: He addresses himself as du — an old-fashioned way of framing a resolution. Lenchen is a diminutive of Lene (Helene): little Lene. aufziehn = aufziehen, to bring up.

sentences.t: Er brachte es also heim, und die zwei Kinder wuchsen mit einander auf.
sentences.l: So he brought it home, and the two children grew up with one another.
sentences.i: So he brought it home, and the two children grew up together.
sentences.n: also is a false friend: it means “so, therefore,” never English “also.” “wuchsen … auf” is aufwachsen, to grow up.

sentences.t: Das aber, das auf dem Baum gefunden worden war, und weil es ein Vogel weggetragen hatte, wurde Fundevogel geheißen.
sentences.l: But the one that had been found on the tree, and because a bird had carried it away, was called Fundevogel.
sentences.i: But the one that had been found up in the tree — and because a bird had carried it off — was named Fundevogel.
sentences.n: The sentence is loosely built: a relative clause and a because-clause hang side by side before the verb arrives. Fundevogel = “found-bird”, from finden and Vogel. We keep the name untranslated, as with all the tales’ names.

sentences.t: Fundevogel und Lenchen hatten sich so lieb, nein so lieb, daß wenn eins das andere nicht sah, ward es traurig.
sentences.l: Fundevogel and Lenchen held each other so dear, no, so dear, that when the one did not see the other, it became sad.
sentences.i: Fundevogel and Lenchen loved each other so dearly — no, so very dearly — that if the one did not see the other, it grew sad.
sentences.n: “sich lieb haben” = to love one another. The “nein so lieb” is the telling breaking off to correct its own measure upward, a spoken gesture kept in print.

sentences.t: Der Förster hatte aber eine alte Köchin, die nahm eines Abends zwei Eimer und fieng an Wasser zu schleppen, und gieng nicht einmal sondern vielemal hinaus an den Brunnen.
sentences.l: But the forester had an old cook; she took two buckets one evening and began to lug water, and went out to the well not once but many times.
sentences.i: But the forester had an old cook, who one evening took two buckets and began hauling water, and went out to the well not once but many times.
sentences.n: “eines Abends” = one evening, a genitive of time. schleppen = to drag, to lug.

sentences.t: Lenchen sah es und sprach „hör einmal, alte Sanne, was trägst du denn so viel Wasser zu?“
sentences.l: Lenchen saw it and said “listen once, old Sanne, why do you carry in so much water then?”
sentences.i: Lenchen saw it and said: “Listen, old Sanne, whatever are you carrying in so much water for?”
sentences.n: “hör einmal” = listen a moment — einmal here softens rather than counts. The was that opens the question is the older “why”, not “what”. denn in a question is the untranslatable “but why…”. “zutragen” = to carry to a place. Sanne is short for Susanne.

sentences.t: „Wenn dus keinem Menschen wieder sagen willst, so will ich dirs wohl sagen.“
sentences.l: “If you will not tell it to any person again, then I will indeed tell it to you.”
sentences.i: “If you will not tell it to a soul, then I will gladly tell you.”
sentences.n: dus = du es, dirs = dir es. “keinem Menschen” = to no person, i.e. to nobody. “wieder sagen” here is to pass on, to repeat.

sentences.t: Da sagte Lenchen nein, sie wollte es keinem Menschen wiedersagen, so sprach die Köchin „morgen früh, wenn der Förster auf die Jagd ist, da koche ich das Wasser, und wenns im Kessel siedet, werfe ich den Fundevogel nein, und will ihn darin kochen.“
sentences.l: Then Lenchen said no, she would not repeat it to any person; so the cook spoke “tomorrow early, when the forester is at the hunt, then I boil the water, and when it seethes in the kettle, I throw Fundevogel in, and will boil him in it.”
sentences.i: Then Lenchen said no, she would not repeat it to a soul; so the cook said: “Tomorrow morning early, when the forester is out hunting, I shall heat the water, and when it seethes in the kettle I shall throw Fundevogel in and boil him in it.”
sentences.n: The nein in “werfe ich den Fundevogel nein” is not “no” but a spoken form of hinein, in — she will throw him in. wollte is the subjunctive of Lenchen’s reported answer; wenns = wenn es.

sentences.t: Des andern Morgens in aller Frühe stieg der Förster auf und gieng auf die Jagd, und als er weg war, lagen die Kinder noch im Bett.
sentences.l: The next morning in all earliness the forester rose up and went to the hunt, and when he was away, the children still lay in bed.
sentences.i: Next morning, very early, the forester got up and went off hunting; and when he was gone the children were still lying in bed.
sentences.n: “des andern Morgens” = on the next morning, a genitive of time. “in aller Frühe” = at the very earliest hour. “aufsteigen” here = to get up out of bed.

sentences.t: Da sprach Lenchen zum Fundevogel „verläßt du mich nicht, so verlaß ich dich auch nicht:“ so sprach der Fundevogel „nun und nimmermehr.“
sentences.l: Then Lenchen spoke to Fundevogel “if you forsake me not, then I forsake you not either:” so Fundevogel spoke “now and nevermore.”
sentences.i: Then Lenchen said to Fundevogel: “If you do not forsake me, I will not forsake you either”; and Fundevogel said: “Now and nevermore.”
sentences.n: A verb-first conditional (“verläßt du mich nicht” = if you do not forsake me), answered by so. “nun und nimmermehr” — now and nevermore: a vow, not a statement. This exchange comes back four times, all but unchanged (the last two open with Fundevogel's name), and is the whole spine of the tale.

sentences.t: Da sprach Lenchen „ich will es dir nur sagen, die alte Sanne schleppte gestern Abend so viel Eimer Wasser ins Haus, da fragte ich sie warum sie das thäte, so sagte sie, wenn ichs keinem Menschen sagen wollte, so wollte sie es mir wohl sagen:
sentences.l: Then Lenchen spoke “I will just tell you: old Sanne dragged so many buckets of water into the house yesterday evening, so I asked her why she was doing that, and she said, if I would tell it to no person, then she would indeed tell it to me:
sentences.i: Then Lenchen said: “Let me just tell you. Old Sanne hauled so many buckets of water into the house yesterday evening, and I asked her why she was doing it; and she said that if I would tell it to nobody, she would gladly tell me.
sentences.n: thäte (modern täte) is the subjunctive of thun/tun, marking the question as reported. From here every verb in Lenchen’s retelling stays in the subjunctive.

sentences.t: sprach ich, ich wollte es gewiß keinem Menschen sagen: da sagte sie, morgen früh, wenn der Vater auf die Jagd wäre, wollte sie den Kessel voll Wasser sieden, dich hineinwerfen und kochen.
sentences.l: said I, I would certainly tell it to no person: then she said, tomorrow early, when father was at the hunt, she would boil the kettle full of water, throw you in and cook you.
sentences.i: So I said I would certainly tell nobody; and then she said that tomorrow morning early, when father was out hunting, she would set the kettle of water seething, throw you in, and boil you.
sentences.n: “sprach ich” with the verb first is a plain narrative speech tag. The dich breaks out of the reported speech and turns straight to Fundevogel — the account and the fright run into each other.

sentences.t: Wir wollen aber geschwind aufsteigen, uns anziehen und zusammen fortgehen.“
sentences.l: But we will get up quickly, dress ourselves and go away together.”
sentences.i: But let us get up quickly, dress, and go away together.”
sentences.n: “wir wollen” + infinitive is the ordinary German “let us…”. geschwind = quick, quickly.

sentences.t: Also standen die beiden Kinder auf, zogen sich geschwind an und giengen fort.
sentences.l: So the two children stood up, dressed themselves quickly and went away.
sentences.i: So the two children got up, dressed quickly, and went away.
sentences.n: Three separable verbs in a row, each with its prefix at the end: standen … auf, zogen sich … an (to dress), giengen fort.

sentences.t: Wie nun das Wasser im Kessel kochte, gieng die Köchin in die Schlafkammer, wollte den Fundevogel holen und ihn hinein werfen.
sentences.l: When now the water was boiling in the kettle, the cook went into the sleeping-chamber, wanted to fetch Fundevogel and throw him in.
sentences.i: Now when the water was boiling in the kettle, the cook went into the sleeping-chamber to fetch Fundevogel and throw him in.
sentences.n: wollen here is less “wanted” than “was about to, meant to”.

sentences.t: Aber, als sie hinein kam und zu den Betten trat, waren die Kinder alle beide fort: da wurde ihr grausam angst, und sie sprach vor sich „was will ich nun sagen, wenn der Förster heim kommt und sieht daß die Kinder weg sind?
sentences.l: But when she came in and stepped to the beds, both the children were gone: then fear came cruelly upon her, and she spoke before herself “what am I to say now, when the forester comes home and sees that the children are away?
sentences.i: But when she came in and stepped to the beds, both the children were gone; and she grew terribly frightened, and said to herself: “What shall I say now, when the forester comes home and sees that the children are gone?
sentences.n: “ihr wurde angst” is impersonal, with the person in the dative: fear came upon her. grausam (cruelly) is here just an intensifier, “terribly”. “vor sich sprechen” = to say to oneself.

sentences.t: Geschwind hinten nach, daß wir sie wieder kriegen.“
sentences.l: Quickly after them, so that we get them back again.”
sentences.i: Quick, after them, so that we get them back!”
sentences.n: A command with no verb at all — “geschwind hinten nach”, quick, after them — the way an order is barked.

sentences.t: Da schickte die Köchin drei Knechte nach, die sollten laufen und die Kinder einlangen.
sentences.l: Then the cook sent three farm-hands after them, who were to run and catch the children up.
sentences.i: Then the cook sent three farm-hands after them, who were to run and overtake the children.
sentences.n: Knecht is a male servant, a farm-hand. “einlangen” here means to reach, to catch up with — a regional use of the verb.

sentences.t: Die Kinder aber saßen vor dem Wald, und als sie die drei Knechte von weitem laufen sahen, sprach Lenchen zum Fundevogel „verläßt du mich nicht, so verlaß ich dich auch nicht.“
sentences.l: But the children sat before the forest, and when they saw the three farm-hands running from afar, Lenchen spoke to Fundevogel “if you forsake me not, then I forsake you not either.”
sentences.i: But the children were sitting before the wood; and when they saw the three farm-hands running in the distance, Lenchen said to Fundevogel: “If you do not forsake me, I will not forsake you either.”
sentences.n: “vor dem Wald” is at the edge of the wood, on the near side of it, not in front of a building. “von weitem” = from a distance.

sentences.t: So sprach Fundevogel „nun und nimmermehr.“
sentences.l: So Fundevogel spoke “now and nevermore.”

sentences.t: Da sagte Lenchen „werde du zum Rosenstöckchen, und ich zum Röschen darauf.“
sentences.l: Then Lenchen said “become you a little rose-stock, and I the little rose upon it.”
sentences.i: Then Lenchen said: “Do you become a little rose-bush, and I the little rose upon it.”
sentences.n: “werden zu” = to turn into. Two diminutives at once: Rosenstöckchen, little rose-stock, and Röschen, little rose. The du after the imperative is emphatic — you be the one.

sentences.t: Wie nun die drei Knechte vor den Wald kamen, so war nichts da als ein Rosenstrauch und ein Röschen oben drauf, die Kinder aber nirgend.
sentences.l: When now the three farm-hands came before the wood, there was nothing there but a rose-bush and a little rose on top of it, but the children nowhere.
sentences.i: Now when the three farm-hands came before the wood, there was nothing there but a rose-bush with a little rose on top of it — and the children nowhere.
sentences.n: als here = except, but. nirgend = modern nirgends, nowhere.

sentences.t: Da sprachen sie „hier ist nichts zu machen,“ und giengen heim und sagten der Köchin sie hätten nichts in der Welt gesehen als nur ein Rosenstöckchen und ein Röschen oben darauf.
sentences.l: Then they spoke “here is nothing to be done,” and went home and told the cook they had seen nothing in the world but only a little rose-stock and a little rose on top of it.
sentences.i: Then they said: “There is nothing to be done here,” and went home and told the cook they had seen nothing in the world but a little rose-bush with a little rose on top of it.
sentences.n: hätten is the subjunctive of reported speech: what the men said they saw.

sentences.t: Da schalt die alte Köchin, „ihr Einfaltspinsel, ihr hättet das Rosenstöckchen sollen entzwei schneiden und das Röschen abbrechen und mit nach Haus bringen, geschwind und thuts.“
sentences.l: Then the old cook scolded, “you simpletons, you should have cut the little rose-stock in two and broken off the little rose and brought it home with you, quick and do it.”
sentences.i: Then the old cook railed at them: “You blockheads! You should have cut the rose-bush in two and broken off the little rose and brought it home with you. Quick now, and do it.”
sentences.n: Einfaltspinsel — literally a “simplicity-brush”, a standing name for a fool. In “hättet das Rosenstöckchen sollen entzwei schneiden” the modal comes before the verb it governs; modern German would end the clause “entzwei schneiden sollen”. thuts = thut es, modern tut es.

sentences.t: Sie mußten also zum zweitenmal hinaus und suchen.
sentences.l: So they had to go out and search a second time.
sentences.n: “zum zweitenmal” = for the second time. After mußten the verb of motion is left out — had to [go] out.

sentences.t: Die Kinder sahen sie aber von weitem kommen, da sprach Lenchen „Fundevogel, verläßt du mich nicht, so verlaß ich dich auch nicht.“
sentences.l: But the children saw them coming from afar; then Lenchen spoke “Fundevogel, if you forsake me not, then I forsake you not either.”
sentences.i: But the children saw them coming in the distance, and Lenchen said: “Fundevogel, if you do not forsake me, I will not forsake you either.”

sentences.t: Fundevogel sagte „nun und nimmermehr.“
sentences.l: Fundevogel said “now and nevermore.”

sentences.t: Sprach Lenchen „so werde du eine Kirche und ich die Krone darin.“
sentences.l: Said Lenchen “then become you a church and I the crown in it.”
sentences.i: Said Lenchen: “Then do you become a church, and I the crown within it.”
sentences.n: What the Krone is here is not certain: it may be the crown-shaped chandelier hung in a church (a Krone or Kronleuchter), or simply a crown among the church treasures. The tale does not say, and the picture is meant to be as odd as it sounds.

sentences.t: Wie nun die drei Knechte dahin kamen, war nichts da als eine Kirche und eine Krone darin.
sentences.l: When now the three farm-hands came there, there was nothing there but a church and a crown in it.

sentences.t: Sie sprachen also zu einander „was sollen wir hier machen, laßt uns nach Hause gehen.“
sentences.l: So they spoke to one another “what are we to do here, let us go home.”
sentences.i: So they said to one another: “What are we to do here? Let us go home.”
sentences.n: “laßt uns” = let us, the plural imperative of lassen.

sentences.t: Wie sie nach Haus kamen, fragte die Köchin ob sie nichts gefunden hätten: so sagten sie nein, sie hätten nichts gefunden als eine Kirche, da wäre eine Krone darin gewesen.
sentences.l: When they came home, the cook asked whether they had found nothing: so they said no, they had found nothing but a church, and a crown had been in it.
sentences.i: When they came home the cook asked whether they had found nothing; and they said no, they had found nothing but a church, and there had been a crown in it.
sentences.n: hätten and wäre keep the whole report in the subjunctive — the men’s words, not the narrator’s.

sentences.t: „Ihr Narren,“ schalt die Köchin, „warum habt ihr nicht die Kirche zerbrochen und die Krone mit heim gebracht?“
sentences.l: “You fools,” scolded the cook, “why did you not break the church to pieces and bring the crown home with you?”
sentences.n: “mit heim gebracht” — heimbringen, to bring home, with mit adding “along with you.”

sentences.t: Nun machte sich die alte Köchin selbst auf die Beine und gieng mit den drei Knechten den Kindern nach.
sentences.l: Now the old cook set herself on her legs and went after the children with the three farm-hands.
sentences.i: Now the old cook took to her own legs and went after the children with the three farm-hands.
sentences.n: “sich auf die Beine machen” = to get oneself moving, to set off on foot.

sentences.t: Die Kinder sahen aber die drei Knechte von weitem kommen, und die Köchin wackelte hinten nach.
sentences.l: But the children saw the three farm-hands coming from afar, and the cook waddled along behind.
sentences.n: wackeln = to wobble, to waddle — the one word the tale spends on the old cook in pursuit.

sentences.t: Da sprach Lenchen „Fundevogel, verläßt du mich nicht, so verlaß ich dich auch nicht.“
sentences.l: Then Lenchen spoke “Fundevogel, if you forsake me not, then I forsake you not either.”
sentences.i: Then Lenchen said: “Fundevogel, if you do not forsake me, I will not forsake you either.”

sentences.t: Da sprach der Fundevogel „nun und nimmermehr.“
sentences.l: Then Fundevogel spoke “now and nevermore.”

sentences.t: Sprach Lenchen „werde zum Teich und ich die Ente drauf.“
sentences.l: Said Lenchen “become a pond and I the duck upon it.”
sentences.n: drauf = darauf, upon it. The tender diminutives of the first shape are long gone: a plain pond, a plain duck, and this time deadly.

sentences.t: Die Köchin aber kam herzu, und als sie den Teich sahe, legte sie sich drüber hin und wollte ihn aussaufen.
sentences.l: But the cook came up, and when she saw the pond, she laid herself down over it and wanted to drink it up.
sentences.i: But the cook came up; and when she saw the pond she lay down over it and meant to drink it dry.
sentences.n: sahe is an older form of sah, saw. saufen (here aussaufen) is drinking as animals drink, and coarse when used of people.

sentences.t: Aber die Ente kam schnell geschwommen, faßte sie mit ihrem Schnabel beim Kopf und zog sie ins Wasser hinein: da mußte die alte Hexe ertrinken.
sentences.l: But the duck came swimming quickly, seized her with its beak by the head and pulled her into the water: then the old witch had to drown.
sentences.i: But the duck came swimming up quickly, seized her by the head with its beak, and dragged her into the water; and so the old witch had to drown.
sentences.n: “kam geschwommen” — a participle after kommen tells how the arrival was made. Only here is the cook called a Hexe, a witch.

sentences.t: Da giengen die Kinder zusammen nach Haus und waren herzlich froh; und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, leben sie noch.
sentences.l: Then the children went home together and were heartily glad; and if they have not died, they are living still.
sentences.n: The closing formula in its short form: “wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, leben sie noch”. The tale declines to say the two are dead, and so they are not.
